chapter: Streetcar, Cab revival shows and trips abroad
title: Subbing with Ellington and his regret about not staying
summary: While at the radio station he replaced Chauncey Haughton for six to eight weeks with Duke Ellington's band at the Hurricane, recommended Jimmy Hamilton, and regrets not staying on.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Yeah. How about the time you played with Ellington?
Now, I was at the radio station when I played with Ellington.
When -- that's one of the only things -- regrets of my life, that I didn't stay with Duke.

Yeah, I was -- I was working at the Hurricane station. Well, Chauncey Hanton was playing with Duke, and he went in the Army, and he didn't have a clarinet player, so they got in touch with me and asked me to come. So I went over there and started to playing. I played, I guess, the whole stay that he was in Hurricane, I imagine about six or eight weeks or something like that. And --

Well, that was -- there was Johnny and Harry and Ben Webster and myself. Well, that was the chair (inaudible), and Duke didn't have first, second and third chairs. They just had guys play -- I was playing tenor. Tenor and doubling on Clarinet

So anyway, after the weeks were over, Duke says, well, you know, we're going to go. You going to stay with the band? I said, well, you know, I thought I had a lifetime job at ABC. So I told him, no, I couldn't go, but I knew a clarinet player, a good clarinet player. And so he said, who's that. I said, Jimmy Hamilton.
So at that time Jimmy had been in New York, but he had gone back to Philly. And we got in touch with Jimmy, and

he came in the band. And after that -- I mean after I left the station and things, well, I said, well, I should have stayed with Duke because I might not have been financially as well off, but I would have made a bigger name for myself as a clarinet player. But that's the way life, you know. Of course, now I think differently it was because I didn't want to be a clarinet player in the first place.

And I had gotten that reputation because about ten years ago I didn't play anything but clarinet, you know, and especially the years when the Central Plaza was running and Metropole and all that, you know.
